_comment: ngsolve time_dependent_ns#6 (the DFG Schafer-Turek benchmark). Run 2026-08-06 on NGSolve 6.2.2604: DFG-2D-1, the steady Re=20 case -- channel 2.2x0.41, cylinder radius 0.05 at (0.2,0.2), nu=1e-3, parabolic inlet with peak 0.3 so the mean is 0.2 and Re = 20. Taylor-Hood on a curved mesh, steady Navier-Stokes through ngsolve.solvers.Newton with inverse='umfpack' (the default factoriser hangs on this saddle-point system), drag and lift from the residual functional tested against a function that is 1 on the cylinder. On 890 elements at order 3 the result is Cd = 5.57988 and Cl = 0.010789, BOTH inside the published bounds Cd in [5.5700,5.5900] and Cl in [0.0104,0.0110] -- the benchmark passing against external numbers, not a self-comparison. Departure from the claim recorded: Cd is far less sensitive than 'values 5%+ off expose a problem' suggests -- the coarsest mesh tried already puts Cd inside the band (5.58727) while its Cl is 0.029599, nearly three times the upper bound, so checking drag alone passes a badly wrong mesh. Replacing the parabolic inlet with a plug of the same mean velocity drops Cd to 4.82471, outside the band, so the benchmark does detect the boundary-condition error the claim says it detects. Mutation: dropping the convective term InnerProduct(Grad(u)*u,v) leaves the Stokes drag and the fixture fails on finest_cd_inside_published_bounds. MUTATION CONTROL (re-runnable): T2_MUTATE=1 drops the convective term InnerProduct(Grad(u)*u, v) from the bilinear form in run(), leaving the Stokes drag -- the missing-convective-term error the claim says this benchmark exposes. Re-verified by execution 2026-08-06 on NGSolve 6.2.2604: the unmutated run matches all 7 expect_in_output strings; T2_MUTATE=1 removes 'finest_cd_inside_published_bounds=True', 'finest_cl_inside_published_bounds=True', 'benchmark_reproduced=True' and 'drag_alone_would_pass_the_coarse_mesh=True' so the fixture goes red. Re-run: T2_MUTATE=1 python source.py
